sections.h2: Your options for selling a Plymouth house
sections.html:
Plymouth homeowners have three practical paths. A full-service listing brings the most showings. Selling on your own spares you the commission, though you handle the pricing and the paperwork. Selling directly to a home-buying company avoids repairs and showings and closes fast, at a lower price.

  • Agent listing: widest exposure, with showings, repairs and a commission attached.
  • Owner-handled sale: no commission, and the negotiating is all yours.
  • Direct sale: the house stays as it is, the closing date is quick, and the price reflects the work a buyer takes on.

A tidy house priced to its neighborhood draws steady interest. Direct sale tends to work better for a house with postponed repairs, sitting tenants or an estate to wrap up.

Plymouth skews toward owners and expensive homes, about 10 miles west of downtown Minneapolis. The 2025 estimate is 2.6% below the April 2020 base, so demand is steady and not climbing fast, and roughly 89% of residents were at the same address the year before.

The city maintains about 300 miles of streets and 863 cul-de-sacs, so many houses sit on quiet curving blocks and not on a grid. Medicine Lake and Parkers Lake are both within the city, and lakeside houses draw their own set of buyers.

School boundaries cut across the city, so the district follows the exact address. Confirm that address before printing a school name in an advertisement.

  • Wayzata Public Schools (ISD 284): serves most of the city, especially the west, northwest and south.
  • Robbinsdale Area Schools (ISD 281): serves the east-central section.
  • Osseo (ISD 279): takes in the northeast.
  • Hopkins (ISD 270): reaches the southeast corner.

Open enrollment lets families choose a district other than the one assigned to their address. Put the district on your listing sheet, since buyers with children weigh it more than most upgrades.

sections.h2: Getting the house ready for an inspector
sections.html: Winters are cold, with average lows near 3 degrees Fahrenheit. Inspectors go straight to the roof, gutters, attic insulation and furnace, so look at those yourself before the first showing. A direct buyer checks the same items and prices them in, so a short list of known problems helps whichever route you take.

sections.h2: If your Plymouth house is a rental
sections.html:
Every Plymouth rental needs a rental dwelling license, from a single-family home to a large complex. One- and two-family homes and condominium units get a three-year license, and other dwelling types renew each year.

City inspectors visit apartment buildings annually and other rental housing every three years. An owner or manager with more than one Plymouth rental has to complete Crime Free Multi-Housing training before renewal. Licenses cannot be transferred or refunded, which means a buyer keeping your tenant must apply in the buyer's own name. Phone the city's Community and Economic Development department at 763-509-5430 for the current fee schedule and for the timing of your next inspection.

The city also has a lodging tax ordinance that applies to short-term rentals. Did you rent the house by the night? Ask the city how that tax applies before closing.

Before the purchase agreement is signed, Minnesota Statutes section 513.55 has you put in writing the facts you know that could significantly hurt an ordinary buyer's enjoyment of the home. Write it honestly, from your own knowledge.

Section 103I.235 adds a well statement. You either list each known well, with its legal description and a map, or state that you know of none. Many sellers can use the short "no known wells" line on the deed, but check the property for an old unsealed well first. At closing, Hennepin County's recording office expects the deed, an electronic certificate of real estate value when the price tops $3,000, a "send tax statements to" address and the well statement.

  • Recording runs $46 per document, with a $5 conservation fee added where state deed tax is paid.
  • A deed cannot be recorded against a parcel carrying delinquent taxes, so clear any balance first.
  • Documents can go in by appointment at the Government Center, through your title company's eRecording, on the county's Virtual Recorder site for a $3 service fee, or by mail.

The county's recording page carries the current fee list and a deed tax calculator.

Plymouth's property tax bill from Hennepin County comes due in spring and fall, on the 15th of May and of October. When the 15th lands on a weekend or holiday, payment is due the following business day. Before you list, confirm the most recent payment posted.

Late payments draw a state penalty that grows each month on the unpaid part. If a lender escrows your taxes, ask the servicer for payoff and escrow refund figures well ahead of closing. The title company then divides the current year's bill by ownership dates. The county's tax payment page explains payment methods, and the property tax line at 612-348-3011 can confirm a parcel's status. If the bill is paid through escrow, you may be owed a refund from the servicer after closing, so keep the servicer's address current. If you pay the bill yourself, keep the receipt for each half, since the title company will ask which payments are already made and a quick answer keeps the closing date on track.

sections.h2: From accepted offer to closing day
sections.html: After you accept a direct offer, the title company runs the search and prepares the deed. Your part is the well statement, an address for future tax statements and a payoff figure from your lender. A rented house also needs the lease details and the license expiration date handed over. At closing the deed is recorded, the year's tax is divided by ownership dates, and you are paid what is left once your mortgage and any unpaid tax are settled. Ask the title company for a copy of the final statement and keep it with your tax records for next year's filing, along with the recorded deed once it comes back.

faqs.q: Do I have to fix anything before selling my Plymouth house?
faqs.a: No, a house can sell in its present condition. You must still give the buyer a written list of material problems you know about. Conventional buyers negotiate over inspection results, while a direct buyer folds repair costs into the price and closes with no fixes from you.

faqs.q: Will my Plymouth rental license pass to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. It cannot be transferred, and the new owner applies for a fresh one. Tell the buyer when yours expires and when the next city inspection falls due.

faqs.q: Which office records a Plymouth deed?
faqs.a: Hennepin County's Recorder and Registrar of Titles, not city hall. Book a time at the Government Center in Minneapolis, mail the deed, have your title company eRecord it, or file online for a $3 service fee.

faqs.q: What if my Plymouth home has back property tax?
faqs.a: The tax and penalties have to be paid before the deed will be recorded, and the title company normally handles that at the closing. Hennepin County's property tax line, 612-348-3011, can give an exact figure.

faqs.q: How do I find out which school district my Plymouth address belongs to?
faqs.a: Ask the district itself. Wayzata, Robbinsdale, Osseo and Hopkins each cover part of Plymouth, with Wayzata taking most of the city. Have the answer ready before your first showing, because buyers with children will ask.
